raw_graphql_pull_request.body:
## Overview

Reworks the HY V4 iHC Triton kernels: `triton_ihc_pre` gets an M-blocked
K-reduction with a split-K path for small token counts, and `triton_ihc_post`
tiles the whole hc dimension at once. No change in numerical output.

## Claims

- **`triton_ihc_pre` is 1.4-2.7x faster from 64 tokens up** — 2.22x at 1024,
  2.33x at 4096, 2.38x at 16384, 2.67x at 32768 (H100, `hidden_size=6144`,
  `hc_mult=4`, bf16).
- **`triton_ihc_post` is 1.04-1.12x from 64 tokens up** — effective bandwidth
  2878 → 3018 GB/s at 16384 tokens, ~90% of H100 HBM3 peak.
- **No accuracy loss** — both kernels match the current ones across 18 token
  counts from 1 to 32768 at `hidden_size` 4096 and 6144; post stays bitwise
  equal to the torch reference.
- **End-to-end +9.4% request throughput and -8.5% median TTFT** for
  1024-token prefill at concurrency 64 on 8×H100, and -2.6% single-request
  TPOT across all four workload shapes tested.
- No regression at any measured shape or workload. Shared memory unchanged
  (12288 B), no register spills.

## Validation

### 1. Kernel microbenchmark

H100 80GB HBM3, `hidden_size=6144` (HY V4's own dimension), `hc_mult=4`, bf16.

| tokens | pre speedup | post speedup |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 64 | **1.37x** | **1.12x** |
| 128 | **1.67x** | **1.12x** |
| 384 | **1.99x** | 1.06x |
| 1024 | **2.22x** | 1.04x |
| 4096 | **2.33x** | 1.05x |
| 16384 | **2.38x** | 1.05x |
| 32768 | **2.67x** | 1.05x |

Still rising at 32768, so larger chunked-prefill batches should gain more.
Below 32 tokens both kernels are within ±5% of the current ones (pre 1.01-1.11x,
post 0.95-0.98x), where absolute times are 3-6 us.

<details>
<summary>Full table with absolute times and timing methodology</summary>

Timed with **CUDA graph replay**. This matters: iterating with a
`synchronize()` per call measures host-side dispatch (~48 us for pre), which
completely buries a 5 us kernel and makes the small-token shapes look like
regressions. Each point is the median of 3 rounds × 200-3000 replays.

| tokens | path | pre before (us) | pre after (us) | pre speedup | post before (us) | post after (us) | post speedup |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | split-K | 5.28 | 5.22 | 1.01x | 3.03 | 3.07 | 0.98x |
| 8 | split-K | 6.12 | 5.50 | 1.11x | 3.03 | 3.17 | 0.95x |
| 64 | split-K | 11.92 | 8.68 | 1.37x | 3.43 | 3.05 | 1.12x |
| 128 | split-K | 19.51 | 11.67 | 1.67x | 4.41 | 3.94 | 1.12x |
| 384 | split-K | 47.68 | 23.94 | 1.99x | 14.62 | 13.80 | 1.06x |
| 512 | M-blocked | 62.49 | 29.55 | 2.11x | 20.87 | 20.04 | 1.04x |
| 1024 | M-blocked | 127.08 | 57.31 | 2.22x | 42.20 | 40.62 | 1.04x |
| 4096 | M-blocked | 504.73 | 216.82 | 2.33x | 159.45 | 152.41 | 1.05x |
| 16384 | M-blocked | 2006.68 | 844.30 | 2.38x | 629.55 | 600.62 | 1.05x |
| 32768 | M-blocked | 4007.95 | 1500.17 | 2.67x | 1263.54 | 1198.35 | 1.05x |

post is 0.95-0.98x below 32 tokens, where the grid cannot fill the GPU and the
absolute difference is 0.15 us.

</details>

### 2. Accuracy — no loss

Every shape was checked against the current kernels before timing.
**All passed, no mismatches.**

<details>
<summary>Tolerances and coverage</summary>

- `triton_ihc_pre`: output matches within `rtol=2e-2, atol=2e-2` (bf16), post
  gates within `rtol=1e-3` (fp32).
- `triton_ihc_post`: matches within `rtol=1e-2, atol=1e-2`, and stays bitwise
  equal to the torch reference — the mul/add remains unfused
  (`enable_fp_fusion=False`).
- Token counts: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 255, 256, 384, 512, 1024, 2048,
  4096, 8192, 16384, 32768 — including both sides of the
  `_MBLOCK_MIN_TOKENS` dispatch boundary (255/256 and 384/512).
- `hidden_size`: 4096 and 6144. `hc_mult`: 4.

</details>

### 3. End-to-end serving

HY V4 needs ~780 GB of weights across two nodes, which was not available, so
the kernels were exercised through **DeepSeek-V4-Flash** — same mHC family,
`hc_mult=4`, hitting the identical kernel specialization. Its mHC call sites
were substituted with the iHC kernels so they run inside a real serving path.

8×H100, TP=8, EP on, `max-num-batched-tokens=8192`, `max-num-seqs=64`.
`vllm bench serve --dataset-name random`, seed 0, **3 runs per point, median
taken** (the first run of each point is 40-56% slower on prefill-heavy shapes,
so single-run numbers are unusable). 2556 requests per version, zero failures.

| workload (in/out) | concurrency | throughput | median TTFT | median TPOT |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1024 / 1 | 64 | **+9.4%** | **-8.5%** | — |
| 1024 / 1 | 32 | **+4.2%** | -4.6% | — |
| 32 / 1024 | 1 | +2.6% | +0.5% | **-2.6%** |
| 1024 / 1024 | 64 | +0.4% | **-8.2%** | 0.0% |
| 16384 / 512 | 1 | +3.0% | **-7.1%** | **-2.7%** |

**No workload regressed.** The prefill-dominated shape gains most, and the
gain grows with concurrency — more tokens per batch is exactly where the
M-blocked path wins.

<details>
<summary>All four workloads, every concurrency level</summary>

**1024 in / 1 out (prefill-dominated)**

| concurrency | requests | req/s before → after | median TTFT (ms) | TTFT P99 (ms) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 16 | 5.57 → 5.76 (+3.4%) | 177.7 → 172.0 (-3.2%) | 185.6 → 180.1 |
| 8 | 128 | 23.15 → 23.20 (+0.2%) | 331.8 → 331.1 (-0.2%) | 385.5 → 385.7 |
| 32 | 512 | 58.96 → 61.47 (+4.2%) | 514.4 → 491.0 (-4.6%) | 633.6 → 597.0 (-5.8%) |
| 64 | 1024 | 99.95 → 109.35 (+9.4%) | 568.4 → 519.9 (-8.5%) | 803.8 → 749.9 (-6.7%) |

Concurrency 8 is flat because 8 × 1024 = 8192 exactly saturates
`max-num-batched-tokens`, so the batch does not grow there.

**32 in / 1024 out (decode-dominated, exercises the split-K path)**

| concurrency | requests | output tok/s before → after | median TPOT (ms) | median TTFT (ms) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 4 | 132.00 → 135.47 (+2.6%) | 7.56 → 7.36 (-2.6%) | 23.9 → 24.0 |
| 16 | 64 | 1554.35 → 1570.80 (+1.1%) | 10.00 → 9.94 (-0.7%) | 243.7 → 209.9 (-13.9%) |
| 64 | 256 | 4738.68 → 4714.96 (-0.5%) | 13.06 → 13.11 (+0.4%) | 388.4 → 378.1 (-2.6%) |

**1024 in / 1024 out (balanced)**

| concurrency | requests | output tok/s before → after | median TPOT (ms) | median TTFT (ms) | TTFT P99 (ms) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 4 | 129.02 → 132.39 (+2.6%) | 7.58 → 7.38 (-2.6%) | 177.6 → 180.9 (+1.8%) | 181.4 → 184.0 |
| 16 | 64 | 1536.71 → 1545.79 (+0.6%) | 10.08 → 10.00 (-0.7%) | 356.9 → 360.4 (+1.0%) | 381.9 → 396.7 |
| 64 | 256 | 4532.83 → 4550.88 (+0.4%) | 13.56 → 13.56 (0.0%) | 567.9 → 521.4 (-8.2%) | 901.5 → 786.8 (-12.7%) |

**16384 in / 512 out (long context)**

| concurrency | requests | output tok/s before → after | median TPOT (ms) | median TTFT (ms) | TTFT P99 (ms) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 4 | 121.73 → 125.37 (+3.0%) | 7.68 → 7.47 (-2.7%) | 285.5 → 265.1 (-7.1%) | 289.6 → 271.9 (-6.1%) |
| 8 | 32 | 813.91 → 824.39 (+1.3%) | 8.77 → 8.66 (-1.2%) | 563.4 → 559.2 (-0.7%) | 833.3 → 825.1 (-1.0%) |

Across 36 metric/concurrency combinations, only 32/1024 at concurrency 64 is
marginally below baseline (throughput -0.5%, TPOT +0.4%), both within the
spread seen across the three rounds.

Single-request TPOT improves 2.6-2.7% in all four workloads (7.56→7.36,
7.58→7.38, 7.68→7.47 ms) with near-zero variance across rounds — the split-K
path's contribution, independent of input or output length.

The gap between the kernel-level 2.3x and the end-to-end 9.4% is expected:
iHC runs twice per decoder layer, but each layer is dominated by MLA attention
and a 256-expert top-6 MoE.

**Reproduction**

```bash
# Server (identical for both versions; only triton_ihc.py differs)
vllm serve /path/to/DeepSeek-V4-Flash \
  --served-model-name dsv4-flash --tensor-parallel-size 8 \
  --enable-expert-parallel --max-model-len 65536 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \
  --max-num-seqs 64 --trust-remote-code --port 8000

# Client, 3x per point; 1024/1 at concurrency 64 shown
vllm bench serve --backend vllm --model /path/to/DeepSeek-V4-Flash \
  --served-model-name dsv4-flash --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 \
  --dataset-name random --random-input-len 1024 --random-output-len 1 \
  --max-concurrency 64 --num-prompts 1024 --seed 0
```

</details>

### 4. Lint

`ruff-check`, `ruff-format`, `typos`, `actionlint`, and `mypy` (3.11) all pass
on the changed file.

## Details

**pre** — stage1 previously re-read the `x` tile once per projection row. It
now blocks over tokens (`_BLOCK_M`) and loads each tile once to feed all
`2*hc_mult` rows. Below `_MBLOCK_MIN_TOKENS` that path starves, so a split-K
variant takes over: one program per `(token, K-chunk)`, all projection rows
read as a single tile.

**post** — pure streaming (`out = post * x + residual`), so only the access
pattern was left. Handling the whole hc dimension as one `[hc, BLOCK_D]` tile
turns the residual loads and stores into single 2D accesses, and a D-major
grid keeps consecutive programs contiguous.

<details>
<summary>Design decisions and tradeoffs</summary>

**Why two pre paths rather than one.** The split-K and M-blocked variants
duplicate the gating math (sigmoid, rsqrt, channel reduction). Merging them
would need a branch inside the kernel, which Triton compiles as both paths
with the union of their register pressure. Measured at the crossover: forcing
both paths at 384 tokens, split-K is 1.17x faster; at 512 M-blocked wins by
1.03x. Keeping them separate costs ~60 lines and keeps each specialization
tight.

**Why fp32 accumulation, not `tl.dot`.** `tl.dot` in bf16 exceeds the gate
tolerance at `K = hc_mult * hidden_size` (24576 for HY V4). Both variants
accumulate in fp32 throughout.

**Why stage2 reduces in index order.** Both variants write per-split private
slots; stage2 sums them by index, so the result does not depend on which block
finishes first. This keeps pre at two launches without a third reduction
kernel, and makes the output reproducible run to run.

**Block sizes**, from a sweep on H100 at `hidden_size=6144`, `hc_mult=4`:

| constant | value | rationale |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `_BLOCK_M` | 32 | with `_BLOCK_K=64`, beats 8/128 by 13-17% between 384 and 32768 tokens |
| `_BLOCK_K` | 64 | shared memory stays at 12288 B (same as 8/128), no spills |
| `_MBLOCK_MIN_TOKENS` | 512 | measured crossover, see above |
| `_POST_BLOCK_D` | 512 | swept 256/512/1024/2048 × 2/4/8 warps; 512/4 optimal at every shape above 32 tokens |

`_BLOCK_M=32` was checked for occupancy before adopting: shared memory is
12288 B (5.3% of H100's 227 KB per-block limit) and the PTX shows zero
register spills, identical to `_BLOCK_M=8` — `BLOCK_M` rising 4x while
`BLOCK_K` halves keeps the `x` tile the same size.

**No host-device sync added.** The dispatch logic is Python integer
arithmetic on shapes; no `.item()`, `.cpu()`, or `.tolist()` on the execution
path.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Pre-existing limitation found while benchmarking</summary>

`_ihc_post_kernel` launches with
`grid = (cdiv(hidden_size, _POST_BLOCK_D), num_tokens)`, placing the token
count on the grid's Y dimension, which CUDA caps at 65535. A single post call
with `num_tokens >= 65536` fails with `CUDA Error: invalid argument`.

**This is unchanged from the current kernel** — both versions share the grid
layout — and is not reachable with the default `max-num-batched-tokens`. pre
is unaffected: its token count is on the X dimension (capped at 2³¹).

Swapping the two dimensions would fix it but inverts the D-major traversal
that this PR's post optimization relies on, so it needs either a blocked
token dimension or a re-measurement of the bandwidth gain. Happy to address
it here or in a follow-up, whichever reviewers prefer.

</details>

---

**pre** — stage1 previously re-read the `x` tile once per projection row. It
now blocks over tokens (`_BLOCK_M`) and loads each tile once to feed all
`2*hc_mult` rows. Below `_MBLOCK_MIN_TOKENS` that path starves, so a split-K
variant takes over: one program per `(token, K-chunk)`, all projection rows
read as a single tile.

**post** — pure streaming (`out = post * x + residual`), so only the access
pattern was left. Handling the whole hc dimension as one `[hc, BLOCK_D]` tile
turns the residual loads and stores into single 2D accesses, and a D-major
grid keeps consecutive programs contiguous.

<details>
<summary>Design decisions and tradeoffs</summary>

**Why two pre paths rather than one.** The split-K and M-blocked variants
duplicate the gating math (sigmoid, rsqrt, channel reduction). Merging them
would need a branch inside the kernel, which Triton compiles as both paths
with the union of their register pressure. Measured at the crossover: forcing
both paths at 384 tokens, split-K is 1.17x faster; at 512 M-blocked wins by
1.03x. Keeping them separate costs ~60 lines and keeps each specialization
tight.

**Why fp32 accumulation, not `tl.dot`.** `tl.dot` in bf16 exceeds the gate
tolerance at `K = hc_mult * hidden_size` (24576 for HY V4). Both variants
accumulate in fp32 throughout.

**Why stage2 reduces in index order.** Both variants write per-split private
slots; stage2 sums them by index, so the result does not depend on which block
finishes first. This keeps pre at two launches without a third reduction
kernel, and makes the output reproducible run to run.

**Block sizes**, from a sweep on H100 at `hidden_size=6144`, `hc_mult=4`:

| constant | value | rationale |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `_BLOCK_M` | 32 | with `_BLOCK_K=64`, beats 8/128 by 13-17% between 384 and 32768 tokens |
| `_BLOCK_K` | 64 | shared memory stays at 12288 B (same as 8/128), no spills |
| `_MBLOCK_MIN_TOKENS` | 512 | measured crossover, see above |
| `_POST_BLOCK_D` | 512 | swept 256/512/1024/2048 × 2/4/8 warps; 512/4 optimal at every shape above 32 tokens |

`_BLOCK_M=32` was checked for occupancy before adopting: shared memory is
12288 B (5.3% of H100's 227 KB per-block limit) and the PTX shows zero
register spills, identical to `_BLOCK_M=8` — `BLOCK_M` rising 4x while
`BLOCK_K` halves keeps the `x` tile the same size.

**No host-device sync added.** The dispatch logic is Python integer
arithmetic on shapes; no `.item()`, `.cpu()`, or `.tolist()` on the execution
path.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Pre-existing limitation found while benchmarking</summary>

`_ihc_post_kernel` launches with
`grid = (cdiv(hidden_size, _POST_BLOCK_D), num_tokens)`, placing the token
count on the grid's Y dimension, which CUDA caps at 65535. A single post call
with `num_tokens >= 65536` fails with `CUDA Error: invalid argument`.

**This is unchanged from the current kernel** — both versions share the grid
layout — and is not reachable with the default `max-num-batched-tokens`. pre
is unaffected: its token count is on the X dimension (capped at 2³¹).

Swapping the two dimensions would fix it but inverts the D-major traversal
that this PR's post optimization relies on, so it needs either a blocked
token dimension or a re-measurement of the bandwidth gain. Happy to address
it here or in a follow-up, whichever reviewers prefer.

</details>
